title: Orsen and the Witness
premise: Beatrix Iversen, host of the true-crime podcast 'The Witness', has spent a decade chasing the 1974 disappearance of her grandmother's neighbor, Elsie Vann — until twin letters arrive: one confessing to Elsie's murder, one promising 'the rest is in the ledger, if you can read it.' Following clues hidden in her late grandmother's household account book, Beatrix uncovers that Elsie faked her death to escape an abusive husband and lived on under a borrowed identity — and that the confessor is Elsie herself, now dying and ready to be found. But someone else received the second letter too: the grandson of the man Elsie fled, who wants the inheritance she took with her. In the flooded cellar of a decommissioned lighthouse keeper's cottage, Beatrix finds Elsie alive at ninety-six, chooses to protect her secret rather than broadcast it, and records instead a final episode about the found family that hid her for fifty years.
about_author: Dominic Galloway is the pen name of a former archivist who spent twelve years cataloguing unclaimed estates before turning to fiction. They write mysteries about paper trails, quiet towns, and the people history files under 'missing.'

chapters.title: Twin Envelopes
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. Between episodes of her flagging podcast, Beatrix receives two letters postmarked the same day: a full confession to the 1974 Vann disappearance, unsigned, and a second note reading only 'the ledger knows where I went.' The beat is vertigo — the case she built her life around just moved.

chapters.title: The Coldest Case
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. She replays her original ten-episode series, auditing her own assumptions about Elsie Vann's drowning. A listener comment from years ago — 'check what she left behind, not what was taken' — suddenly reads differently. Beat: the investigator becomes the investigated.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Hand
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. Sorting her late grandmother Maren's boxes, Beatrix finds the household ledger: decades of grocery sums, coal prices — and columns of figures that don't add up, each discrepancy keyed to dates after Elsie vanished. Beat: grief braided with discovery; Maren knew something.

chapters.title: A Man Named Hollis
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. Research identifies Elsie's husband, Gerald Vann, dead since 1989 — but his obituary names a son, Hollis, still living two counties over. When Beatrix cold-calls him, he hangs up mid-sentence after hearing the word 'ledger.' Beat: first open hostility.

chapters.title: What the Sums Hid
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. Decoding the ledger against old tide tables and ferry manifests, she realizes the errant numbers encode payments — someone in town funded a life elsewhere, monthly, for years. Beat: the thrill of pattern, shadowed by the question of who paid and why.

chapters.title: The Ferryman's Daughter
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix interviews Ruth, 88, daughter of the former ferry operator, who goes pale at Elsie's name and admits only: 'My father carried more than passengers some nights.' She warns Beatrix off. Beat: the town's protective silence revealed as loyalty, not complicity.

chapters.title: Hollis Comes Calling
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. Hollis Vann appears at her studio, charming and wrong, asking what she knows about his father's 'stolen estate.' He mentions the second letter — he got one too. Beat: dread; Beatrix realizes she's in a race she didn't know had started.

chapters.title: Episode Eleven
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. Pressured by her producer to milk the confession for ratings, Beatrix records a teaser and then deletes it, unable to say aloud what she suspects: that Elsie may have chosen to disappear. Beat: conscience versus career; the podcaster edits herself.

chapters.title: Maren's Margin
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. A pencil notation in Maren's handwriting — coordinates disguised as a hymn number — points to the decommissioned Gullwatch light station. Beatrix drives out through fog and finds the keeper's cottage sealed, its cellar door bricked sometime in the seventies. Beat: awe curdling into fear.

chapters.title: Someone Else Is Reading
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. Returning to town, she finds her apartment searched — nothing taken but photocopies of ledger pages. Her producer admits he mentioned the case to a 'documentary contact': Hollis. Beat: betrayal close to home; the hunt has inverted.

chapters.title: Ruth Breaks
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. Confronted with the break-in, Ruth finally tells it: her father ferried a terrified young woman across the bay in 1974, and Maren Iversen organized everything after — money, papers, silence. 'We didn't hide a murder,' Ruth says. 'We hid a rescue.' Beat: the case flips entirely.

chapters.title: The Life She Borrowed
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. Tracing the encoded payments forward, Beatrix finds Elsie became 'Edith Marsh,' a schoolteacher in a coastal village three hours north — retired, respected, and, per a nursing home inquiry, possibly still alive at ninety-six. Beat: hope, sharp and fragile.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. At the nursing home, Edith Marsh's room is empty; staff mention a 'grandson' who visited yesterday and left with her 'for a family matter.' Hollis has her. Beat: gut-drop escalation — this is no longer about paper.

chapters.title: The Confession Letter, Again
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. Forensic re-reading of the confession reveals it was written by a shaking hand over many sittings — not guilt, but preparation. Postscripted in different ink: 'If you are reading this, Bea, I ran out of time. Forgive the theater. It was the only door left.' Beat: Elsie planned all of this as a summons.

chapters.title: Gullwatch
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. Beatrix races back to the lighthouse, guessing Elsie's true refuge was always the cottage Maren kept stocked. Inside the bricked cellar, freshly broken open, signs of a struggle — and Hollis waiting in the dark with questions and a crowbar. Beat: confrontation without resolution; he wants the 'inheritance' he believes Elsie stole.

chapters.title: Ninety-Six
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix and alternating fragments of Elsie's dictated memoir. Flashback chapters interleave: young Elsie's marriage, the night she staged the drowning, Maren's cold fury and fiercer loyalty. Beat: the victim becomes the author of her own story.

chapters.title: The Ledger Explained
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. Hidden in the cottage, Elsie explains the ledger was Maren's double-entry: real accounts for the town, coded ones for her new life. The 'inheritance' Hollis seeks never existed — it was grocery money and courage. Beat: deflation of his myth; rage turning desperate.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. A storm seals the coast road; Hollis, humiliated and cornered, blocks the cottage exit, insisting Elsie sign over 'what's owed.' Beatrix records everything on her running recorder. Beat: siege tension; the witness must decide when to stop observing.

chapters.title: What Was Owed
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. Beatrix plays back fifty years of evidence — Ruth's testimony, the ledger, Elsie's own voice — and forces Hollis to hear what his father was. Shaken by the recording and the arriving coast guard called via the lighthouse's restored radio, he breaks. Beat: climax; truth as the weapon.

chapters.title: The Last Episode
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. Instead of exposing Elsie, Beatrix airs a final episode: 'The Witness,' telling the story of a town that hid a woman to save her, names changed, ending unresolved to the public. Beat: sacrifice of the scoop for the person; identity reclaimed on her own terms.

chapters.title: Edith Marsh, In Full
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. Weeks later, Elsie — legally restored to her own name with Ruth's help — moves into Maren's old house with Beatrix as her reluctant landlady-turned-family. Hollis faces charges for the break-in and abduction attempt. Beat: warmth; found family assembled from wreckage.

chapters.title: Closing the Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. Beatrix balances Maren's final coded column and finds the last entry isn't money at all: 'For the girl who stayed gone so she could stay alive. Paid in full.' She closes the book, opens a blank notebook, and begins again. Beat: inheritance understood — not what's left behind, but what's carried forward.
